subject: MAT
label: Grade 12 Science
task: Meet the outcome of every unit in Grade 12 Science Mathematics, and keep one piece of evidence for each.
condition: A 36-week school year, 7 units, a teacher or guide, a learning book or device, and local examples in the local language first with English support.
standard: Each unit: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown. Course pass: no unit at 'Not yet' after one retry, and a pass in SA1 and SA2.

modules.title: Relations, functions and inverse trigonometric functions
modules.outcome: define and graph functions and their inverses
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Relations, functions and inverse trigonometric functions', taught in a way that is with exam-style questions and written reasoning. The target is clear: define and graph functions and their inverses. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Show it with objects or a picture: build or draw the idea in 'Relations, functions and inverse trigonometric functions' before using symbols.
Say the rule in your own words, then write one worked line, naming each step.
Use it: define and graph functions and their inverses. Start with one easy question, then one with a real-life story.
Check it: use a second method, estimate, or work backwards to test your answer.
modules.example: Solved: Right triangle, opposite side 3, hypotenuse 5, adjacent side 4. sin = 3/5 = 0.6, cos = 4/5 = 0.8, tan = 3/4 = 0.75. Method: Model run for 'Relations, functions and inverse trigonometric functions'. Read the question and underline what is asked. Draw or write what is known. Choose the method named in the unit. Work it line by line, one idea per line, with units where they apply. Estimate first so the answer can be tested for sense. Check by working backwards. What a good answer looks like: correct method, every step visible, units stated, and a one-line check.
modules.activity: About 40 to 50 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a timed paper and an error log.
modules.standard: Define and graph functions and their inverses: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Find an inverse: f(x) = 2x - 3. Put y = 2x - 3, solve for x: x = (y + 3)/2. So the inverse is f^-1(x) = (x + 3)/2. Check: f(f^-1(5)) = f(4) = 5.
Step 2, Composition: f(x) = x + 1 and g(x) = x^2. Then (f o g)(2) = f(4) = 5 while (g o f)(2) = g(3) = 9. Composition is not commutative, so order matters.
Step 3, Principal values: sin^-1(1/2) = pi/6, cos^-1(-1/2) = 2 pi/3, tan^-1(1) = pi/4. The ranges are [-pi/2, pi/2] for sin^-1, [0, pi] for cos^-1.
Step 4, Pitfall: sin^-1(sin(5 pi/6)) is not 5 pi/6, since 5 pi/6 is outside the range. sin(5 pi/6) = 1/2, so the answer is sin^-1(1/2) = pi/6.

Step 5, Equivalence relation: R on integers, a R b if a - b is divisible by 3. Reflexive: a - a = 0. Symmetric: if 3 divides a - b it divides b - a. Transitive: sum of two multiples of 3 is a multiple of 3.
Step 6, Your turn: find the inverse of f(x) = 3x + 6 and tan^-1(root 3). Answer: x = (y - 6)/3, so f^-1(x) = (x - 6)/3; and tan^-1(root 3) = pi/3.

modules.title: Matrices and determinants
modules.outcome: operate on matrices and find inverses
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Matrices and determinants', taught in a way that is with exam-style questions and written reasoning. The target is clear: operate on matrices and find inverses. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Show it with objects or a picture: build or draw the idea in 'Matrices and determinants' before using symbols.
Say the rule in your own words, then write one worked line, naming each step.
Use it: operate on matrices and find inverses. Start with one easy question, then one with a real-life story.
Check it: use a second method, estimate, or work backwards to test your answer.
modules.example: Solved: [1 2; 3 4] + [0 1; 1 0] = [1 3; 4 4]. The determinant of [1 2; 3 4] = 1 x 4 - 2 x 3 = -2. Method: Model run for 'Matrices and determinants'. Read the question and underline what is asked. Draw or write what is known. Choose the method named in the unit. Work it line by line, one idea per line, with units where they apply. Estimate first so the answer can be tested for sense. Check by working backwards. What a good answer looks like: correct method, every step visible, units stated, and a one-line check.
modules.activity: About 40 to 50 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a timed paper and an error log.
modules.standard: Operate on matrices and find inverses: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Determinant and inverse: A = [[2, 1], [5, 3]] has det = 2 x 3 - 1 x 5 = 1. The inverse is (1/1) x [[3, -1], [-5, 2]]. Swap the diagonal, change the sign of the other entries.
Step 2, Check: A x A^-1 = [[2 x 3 + 1 x (-5), 2 x (-1) + 1 x 2], [5 x 3 + 3 x (-5), 5 x (-1) + 3 x 2]] = [[1, 0], [0, 1]]. It gives the identity matrix, so the inverse is right.
Step 4, Check: x = 3, y = 1 gives 6 + 1 = 7 and 15 + 3 = 18. Both equations hold. A zero determinant would mean no unique solution.

Step 5, Triangular determinant: for [[1, 2, 3], [0, 1, 4], [0, 0, 2]] the determinant is the product of the diagonal, 1 x 1 x 2 = 2. Expanding along the first column gives the same, 1 x (1 x 2 - 4 x 0) = 2.
Step 6, Your turn: find the determinant and inverse of [[4, 3], [2, 2]]. Answer: det = 8 - 6 = 2; inverse = 1/2 x [[2, -3], [-2, 4]] = [[1, -3/2], [-1, 2]].

modules.title: Continuity, differentiability and applications of derivatives
modules.outcome: differentiate and find maxima and minima
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Continuity, differentiability and applications of derivatives', taught in a way that is with exam-style questions and written reasoning. The target is clear: differentiate and find maxima and minima. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Show it with objects or a picture: build or draw the idea in 'Continuity, differentiability and applications of derivatives' before using symbols.
Say the rule in your own words, then write one worked line, naming each step.
Use it: differentiate and find maxima and minima. Start with one easy question, then one with a real-life story.
Check it: use a second method, estimate, or work backwards to test your answer.
modules.example: Solved: d/dx of (3x squared + 5x) = 6x + 5; at x = 2 the gradient is 17. Limit as x goes to 2 of (x squared - 4)/(x - 2) = limit of (x + 2) = 4. Method: Model run for 'Continuity, differentiability and applications of derivatives'. Read the question and underline what is asked. Draw or write what is known. Choose the method named in the unit. Work it line by line, one idea per line, with units where they apply. Estimate first so the answer can be tested for sense. Check by working backwards. What a good answer looks like: correct method, every step visible, units stated, and a one-line check.
modules.activity: About 40 to 50 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a timed paper and an error log.
modules.standard: Differentiate and find maxima and minima: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Continuity: f(x) = (x^2 - 9)/(x - 3) for x not equal to 3, and f(3) = 6. The limit as x approaches 3 is x + 3 = 6, which equals f(3), so f is continuous at 3.
Step 2, Chain rule: y = (3x + 1)^5 gives dy/dx = 5(3x + 1)^4 x 3 = 15(3x + 1)^4. Also d/dx of e^(2x) = 2e^(2x). Differentiate the outer function, then multiply by the inner derivative.
Step 3, Maxima and minima: f(x) = x^3 - 3x + 2. f'(x) = 3x^2 - 3 = 0 gives x = 1 or -1. f''(x) = 6x. At x = 1, f'' = 6 > 0, a minimum with f(1) = 0. At x = -1, f'' = -6 < 0, a maximum with f(-1) = 4.
Step 4, Check values: f(1) = 1 - 3 + 2 = 0 and f(-1) = -1 + 3 + 2 = 4. Also f(0) = 2 lies between them, as expected for the curve between the turning points.
Step 5, Optimisation: a rectangle has perimeter 40, so sides x and 20 - x. Area A = x(20 - x), A' = 20 - 2x = 0, so x = 10 and A = 100. It is a square, and A'' = -2 < 0.
Step 6, Your turn: find the minimum of x^2 - 6x + 5. Answer: f' = 2x - 6 = 0 gives x = 3, f'' = 2 > 0, and f(3) = 9 - 18 + 5 = -4.

modules.title: Integrals and applications of integrals
modules.outcome: integrate and find areas under curves
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Integrals and applications of integrals', taught in a way that is with exam-style questions and written reasoning. The target is clear: integrate and find areas under curves. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Show it with objects or a picture: build or draw the idea in 'Integrals and applications of integrals' before using symbols.
Say the rule in your own words, then write one worked line, naming each step.
Use it: integrate and find areas under curves. Start with one easy question, then one with a real-life story.
Check it: use a second method, estimate, or work backwards to test your answer.
modules.example: Solved: The integral of (6x + 5) dx = 3x squared + 5x + C. Check by differentiating: 6x + 5. Method: Model run for 'Integrals and applications of integrals'. Read the question and underline what is asked. Draw or write what is known. Choose the method named in the unit. Work it line by line, one idea per line, with units where they apply. Estimate first so the answer can be tested for sense. Check by working backwards. What a good answer looks like: correct method, every step visible, units stated, and a one-line check.
modules.activity: About 40 to 50 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a timed paper and an error log.
modules.standard: Integrate and find areas under curves: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Basic integral: the integral of 3x^2 + 2x + 1 dx = x^3 + x^2 + x + C. And the integral of sin 2x dx = -cos 2x / 2 + C. Differentiate to check: d/dx of -cos 2x / 2 = sin 2x.
Step 2, Substitution: the integral of 2x(x^2 + 1)^3 dx. Let u = x^2 + 1, then du = 2x dx. The integral becomes u^3 du = u^4/4 + C = (x^2 + 1)^4 / 4 + C.
Step 3, Definite integral: from 0 to 1 of x^2 dx = [x^3/3] = 1/3. From 0 to 2 of 3x^2 + 1 dx = [x^3 + x] = 8 + 2 = 10.
Step 4, Area under y = x^2 from 0 to 3: the integral is [x^3/3] from 0 to 3 = 27/3 = 9 square units. Rough check: the curve is below the line y = 3x, whose area is 13.5.
Step 5, Area between curves: y = x and y = x^2 meet at x = 0 and x = 1, with the line above. Area = integral of (x - x^2) = [x^2/2 - x^3/3] = 1/2 - 1/3 = 1/6.
Step 6, Your turn: integrate cos 3x and evaluate the integral of 2x from 0 to 3. Answer: sin 3x / 3 + C; and [x^2] from 0 to 3 = 9.

modules.title: Differential equations
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Differential equations', taught in a way that is with exam-style questions and written reasoning. The target is clear: solve first-order differential equations. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Show it with objects or a picture: build or draw the idea in 'Differential equations' before using symbols.
Say the rule in your own words, then write one worked line, naming each step.
Use it: solve first-order differential equations. Start with one easy question, then one with a real-life story.
Check it: use a second method, estimate, or work backwards to test your answer.
modules.example: Solved: dy/dx = 2x gives y = x squared + C. If y = 3 when x = 0, then C = 3. Method: Model run for 'Differential equations'. Read the question and underline what is asked. Draw or write what is known. Choose the method named in the unit. Work it line by line, one idea per line, with units where they apply. Estimate first so the answer can be tested for sense. Check by working backwards. What a good answer looks like: correct method, every step visible, units stated, and a one-line check.
modules.activity: About 40 to 50 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a timed paper and an error log.
modules.standard: Solve first-order differential equations: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Order and degree: (d^2y/dx^2)^3 + dy/dx = 0 has highest derivative d^2y/dx^2, so order 2, and that derivative is raised to power 3, so degree 3.
Step 2, Direct integration: dy/dx = 2x gives y = x^2 + C. With y(0) = 3 we get C = 3, so y = x^2 + 3. Check: derivative 2x, and y(0) = 3.
Step 3, Separable: dy/dx = x/y gives y dy = x dx. Integrate: y^2/2 = x^2/2 + c, so y^2 = x^2 + k. At (0, 2), k = 4, so y^2 = x^2 + 4.
Step 4, Exponential: dy/dx + 2y = 0 gives dy/y = -2 dx, so ln|y| = -2x + c and y = Ce^(-2x). With y(0) = 5, C = 5. Check: y' = -10e^(-2x) and 2y = 10e^(-2x), which sum to 0.
Step 5, Growth model: dy/dx = ky has solution y = Ae^(kx). If a population of 1,000 grows with k = 0.1, then after 10 time units y = 1,000 x e^1, about 2,718.
Step 6, Your turn: solve dy/dx = 3x^2 with y(1) = 2, and give the general solution of dy/dx = 4y. Answer: y = x^3 + C, then 1 + C = 2 so y = x^3 + 1; and y = Ae^(4x).

modules.title: Vectors and three-dimensional geometry
modules.outcome: use dot and cross products and equations of lines and planes
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Vectors and three-dimensional geometry', taught in a way that is with exam-style questions and written reasoning. The target is clear: use dot and cross products and equations of lines and planes. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Show it with objects or a picture: build or draw the idea in 'Vectors and three-dimensional geometry' before using symbols.
Say the rule in your own words, then write one worked line, naming each step.
Use it: use dot and cross products and equations of lines and planes. Start with one easy question, then one with a real-life story.
Check it: use a second method, estimate, or work backwards to test your answer.
modules.example: Solved: a = (2, 3) and b = (1, -1). a + b = (3, 2). Twice a = (4, 6). Method: Model run for 'Vectors and three-dimensional geometry'. Read the question and underline what is asked. Draw or write what is known. Choose the method named in the unit. Work it line by line, one idea per line, with units where they apply. Estimate first so the answer can be tested for sense. Check by working backwards. What a good answer looks like: correct method, every step visible, units stated, and a one-line check.
modules.activity: About 40 to 50 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a timed paper and an error log.
modules.standard: Use dot and cross products and equations of lines and planes: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Dot product: a = (1, 2, 3) and b = (2, -1, 4). a.b = 1 x 2 + 2 x (-1) + 3 x 4 = 2 - 2 + 12 = 12. And |a| = root of 1 + 4 + 9 = root 14.
Step 3, Angle: |b| = root of 4 + 1 + 16 = root 21. So cos theta = 12 / root 294, about 12 / 17.15 = 0.70, and theta is about 45.6 degrees.
Step 4, Line: through (1, 2, 3) with direction (2, 1, -1): (x - 1)/2 = (y - 2)/1 = (z - 3)/(-1). Setting each ratio to t gives x = 1 + 2t, y = 2 + t, z = 3 - t.
Step 5, Plane: through (1, 0, 0) with normal (2, 3, 1): 2(x - 1) + 3y + z = 0, so 2x + 3y + z = 2. Its distance from the origin is 2/root 14, about 0.53.
Step 6, Your turn: find the dot and cross product of (1, 0, 2) and (3, 1, -1). Answer: dot = 3 + 0 - 2 = 1; cross = (0 - 2, 6 + 1, 1 - 0) = (-2, 7, 1), and (1, 0, 2) . (-2, 7, 1) = 0.

modules.title: Linear programming and probability
modules.outcome: solve optimisation and conditional probability problems
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Linear programming and probability', taught in a way that is with exam-style questions and written reasoning. The target is clear: solve optimisation and conditional probability problems. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Show it with objects or a picture: build or draw the idea in 'Linear programming and probability' before using symbols.
Say the rule in your own words, then write one worked line, naming each step.
Use it: solve optimisation and conditional probability problems. Start with one easy question, then one with a real-life story.
Check it: use a second method, estimate, or work backwards to test your answer.
modules.example: Solved: A fair die has 6 faces and 3 are even, so P(even) = 3/6 = 1/2. Method: Model run for 'Linear programming and probability'. Read the question and underline what is asked. Draw or write what is known. Choose the method named in the unit. Work it line by line, one idea per line, with units where they apply. Estimate first so the answer can be tested for sense. Check by working backwards. What a good answer looks like: correct method, every step visible, units stated, and a one-line check.
modules.activity: About 40 to 50 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a timed paper and an error log.
modules.standard: Solve optimisation and conditional probability problems: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Set up: maximise Z = 4x + 3y subject to 2x + y <= 10, x + 2y <= 8, x, y >= 0. The corner points are (0, 0), (5, 0), (0, 4), and the meeting point of the two lines.
Step 2, Intersection: from 2x + y = 10, y = 10 - 2x. Substitute into x + 2y = 8: x + 20 - 4x = 8, so x = 4 and y = 2. Check: 8 + 2 = 10 and 4 + 4 = 8.
Step 3, Evaluate Z: (0, 0) gives 0, (5, 0) gives 20, (0, 4) gives 12, (4, 2) gives 16 + 6 = 22. The maximum is 22 at (4, 2). Your answer must come from a corner of the region.
Step 4, Conditional probability: P(A) = 0.6, P(B) = 0.5, P(A and B) = 0.3. Then P(A given B) = 0.3/0.5 = 0.6 = P(A), and 0.6 x 0.5 = 0.3, so A and B are independent.

Step 5, Total probability: bag 1 has 3 red and 2 black, bag 2 has 1 red and 4 black, and a bag is chosen at random. P(red) = 1/2 x 3/5 + 1/2 x 1/5 = 4/10 = 2/5. By Bayes, P(bag 1 given red) = (3/10)/(4/10) = 3/4.
Step 6, Your turn: maximise Z = 2x + 3y with x + y <= 5, x <= 3. Answer: corners (0,0), (3,0), (3,2), (0,5) give 0, 6, 12, 15, so the maximum is 15 at (0, 5).
